title: My Three Amigos: How Sweller, Rosenshine, and Ausubel Will Ride With Me Next Year
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: A teacher writing as SoL in the Wild combines the ideas of Sweller, Rosenshine and Ausubel into a reusable ten-step explicit instruction structure called the Three Amigos Model. The post walks through a worked lesson on how population density affects land use in Japan, giving timings for each step, from retrieval-based daily review and an advance organizer to hinge questions, guided reading, concept mapping and an exit ticket. Each step is annotated with which theorist's principle supports it. The author argues the structure is purposeful, reusable across concepts and aligned with cognitive science. The evidence is the author's own planning and design rather than results, and much of the post is a step list.
points: Sweller supplies load management, Rosenshine supplies explicit instruction and review, and Ausubel supplies anchoring new learning to prior knowledge.
The model sequences retrieval, an advance organizer with a bullet-proof definition, vocabulary pre-teaching, hinge questions, guided reading, concept mapping and independent practice.
A single worked lesson on population density in Japan shows each step timed and tied to a theorist.
Many strategies are supported by more than one theorist, and the overlap is presented as the framework's strength.
quotes: Like a lot of teachers, I’ve spent time this summer trying to get better at my craft. I’ve been reading, thinking, and, to be honest, reimagining how I structure my lessons entirely. And three names are central to this reinterpretation of my instruction: John Sweller, Barak Rosenshine, and David Ausubel. Each of them offers something powerful, but taken together? They’re my Three Amigos riding shotgun with me into next year’s classroom.

Looking back at this lesson on how population density affects land use in Japan, I can see how intentionally layering the work of my three amigos, Sweller, Rosenshine, and Ausubel, elevates both the my design, delivery and the work students are completing. From the daily retrieval questions to the carefully placed hinge questions and the co-constructed concept map, every move is purposeful. Each step aims to reduce cognitive overload, connect new ideas to prior knowledge, and guide students from surface-level recall to deep understanding.
What excites me most is how reusable this structure is day to day. I now have a framework that’s both research-informed and classroom-tested.

Each strategy in the chart is something any teacher can implement, and next to it, I’ve noted which of the three theorists supports it and why. Sometimes, a strategy is backed by more than one. That’s the beauty of this “Three Amigos” framework: the overlap reinforces what great teaching looks like. Whether it’s using retrieval practice, using a bullet-proof definition, or gradually releasing responsibility through concept mapping, this toolbox will help me, and hopefully other teachers, align what we do in the classroom with what cognitive science says works best for learning.

This post is a walk-through of a “Three Amigos” inspired explicit instruction structure I’ve built using a concept I’ll be teaching next year in my population unit: How does population density affect land use in Japan? I’m using it to show exactly how I plan to bring the theories and ideas of my amigos to life, step by step in all my lessons regardless of concept with the “Three Amigos Model.
